name: National Indigenous Women's Resource Center
head: NIWRC: what they want, what they hate, how they feel about us
about: NIWRC is a national, Native women-led organization working to advance safety for Native women and communities, rooted in Tribal sovereignty. It runs Women Are Sacred, its national conference held every two years. Day-to-day: Miranda Raney (Director of Communications) and Cory Johnson (Marketing and Communications). CEO: Lucy Simpson. Board Chair: tai simpson (lowercase). Our lead: Nick. Atdhe takes over the account after the 9 Oct Oklahoma City shoot.

rel.note: Miranda likes the direction (29 Sep) and answered our branding ask within 90 minutes (8 Oct). A wrong name on a cut they posted is still fresh (23 Sep).

ver.note: Last 90 days: 5 cuts, all approved at V1. Small sample (n=5). Agency average V1.96, with 50% of cuts going past V1.

read.note: They approve fast when the cut tells their story with dignity. They push back on any image of harm, any stereotype and any wrong name.

quotes.q: I don't think the viewer needs to like see violence to understand that we're talking about violence.
I really want to avoid like crying, cowering women, grabbing hands, hands over mouth, like traditional victim stock imagery.
I like the direction, like with the updates that we went…
I wanted to confirm how you all are identifying folks? … How are we QAing these?

loves: Real Native people, families and community, telling NIWRC's story.
Symbolic imagery: a home for safety, the red dress for MMIW.
Culture shown with care: beadwork, gathering, relatives.
Closer face shots over wide, zoomed-out ones.
“Native women-led” said out loud, not only implied.
Text on screen when there is no good image.
hates: Victim stock imagery: crying, cowering, hands over mouths, chains.
The red handprint. Use the red dress instead.
Wrong names or titles on screen. Tribal affiliations in titles.
Generic or non-US “Native-inspired” footage and music.
Cuts that read like an event recap instead of a story.
Duotone over photos. Music that fights the voice.
how_to_cut: Dignity first. Never show a woman in fear or harm.
Every visual tells the story. Imagery is never decoration.
Names and titles exactly as NIWRC gives them. No Tribal affiliation in titles.
Capital T in “Tribal”, every time. Numbers as numerals: “4 in 5 Native women”.
Music: Native only if made and performed by a verified U.S.-based Native artist, else neutral instrumental.
Captions on all long-form video, over footage only, never over graphic slides.
Footage must be relevant to U.S. Tribal Nations.

perf.note: Instagram @niwrc reels, last 90 days. 66,930 followers. Public data, views only. Only 4 reels were posted in the window. Tap a reel to watch it.

rows.t: “Native women in leadership roles exist everywhere” (DVAM)

perf.foot: A Native woman speaking about leadership did 2.5× the next reel. Our Specialty Institute recap is second. Their Women Are Sacred 2027 Save the Date image (1 Oct) has 1,194 likes, so the teasers land on an audience that already cares.

brand.note: No brand hex codes are written in the client file. Rules on file: white logo on a red background for contrast; a lighter base, not cream; no duotone over photographs. Women Are Sacred 2027: was_lockup1.png is the new lockup (the old two-women-holding-hands lockup is retired), Luminos Marker is the supporting typeface, theme “Weaving Our Future to Safety”, artwork “We Are All Connected” by issitohbi.

## 🎯 Goals & Preferences
- **VISUAL RULE, standing as of 2026-09-29 (Fathom 187924039):** no victim stock imagery in any NIWRC cut — no crying women, no hands over mouths, nothing depicting a woman in fear or harm. Use symbolic or environmental imagery instead: a house exterior for safety, **the red dress (NOT the red handprint) for MMIW**, movement rather than a distressed person for trafficking. Text-on-screen is an acceptable substitute. This applies to every future deliverable, not just the Safety video.

- **North-star story angle:** NIWRC is a **national** organization — every visual must **tell the story**, not merely *represent* Native imagery. Client, 7/14 (verbatim): _"I want to be sure each visual is helping tell the story, rather than simply representing Native imagery… imagery of Native people, families, communities, and cultural connection might create a more direct emotional and narrative link."_ Symbolic montages (Tribal flags) need an explicit narrative reason or they read as decoration.
- **Messaging frame (mid-rebrand):** moving from "ending gender-based violence" → **"advancing safety broadly"** (safe housing, economic security, health, healing, culture, justice). Safety is inseparable from **Tribal sovereignty** — that link is the spine of the Safety Framework pieces.
- **Footage sourcing (hard preference):** **no generic stock imagery.** All footage must be vetted for **US tribal-nation relevance** (NIWRC is the SME and will guide). Culturally-vetted Native B-roll is scarce — this has repeatedly gated edits (7/2 hold; 7/14 museum-b-roll gate). Prefer client-supplied footage; when a shot is stock, expect it to be challenged.
- **On-camera preferences:** show **female dancers where possible**; **avoid the dancer clips from that conference**; prefer closer face shots over wide/zoomed-out ones.
- **Design prefs:** **no duotone over photographs**; drop headers that don't add value; **white logo on a red background** for contrast; lighter base rather than cream; on-screen pull-out words must match the VO.
- **Numbers/coping style:** "4 in 5 Native women" (numerals), NOT "four in five American Indian and Alaska Native women" (7/21 live edit).
